properties.title: M 6.8 - The 2026 Kumamoto Region, Japan Earthquake

contents.bytes:
Key Points

  • A magnitude 6.8 earthquake occurred south of Kumamoto, Japan.
  • The USGS assesses that extensive damage is possible and the disaster is likely widespread. Approximately 1,200,000 people experienced Very Strong (MMI VII) to Severe (MMI VIII) shaking.
  • Landslides and liquefaction triggered by this earthquake are estimated to be significant in severity and/or spatial extent.
  • If you experienced this earthquake, please tell us about it with the Did You Feel It? survey.
  • The USGS magnitude of 6.8 (Mww) differs from the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) magnitude 7.1 (Mj) primarily because the agencies are reporting different magnitude types. When the methods for calculating magnitude differ significantly, they are considered to be different magnitude types. For this event, the JMA is reporting a local magnitude (Mj), while the USGS is reporting a moment magnitude (Mww). Earthquakes are complex phenomena, and using a single number to represent earthquake size is a simplification. Different magnitude types capture different characteristics of earthquake source processes, and some techniques have operational advantages, such as faster calculation or the ability to more accurately estimate the size of large earthquakes.

Tectonic Summary

The July 28, 2026, M 6.8 earthquake south of Kumamoto, on the island of Kyushu in southwest Japan, occurred as the result of shallow strike‑slip faulting. Focal mechanisms indicate that the slip took place either on a left‑lateral fault striking northwest or on a right‑lateral fault striking northeast. Most seismicity in the Kyushu region is associated with the deep subduction of the Philippine Sea plate. While the earthquake occurred several hundred kilometers northwest of the Ryukyu Trench, where the Philippine Sea plate begins its northwestward subduction beneath Japan and the Eurasia plate, the shallow depth and faulting style of this event indicate it occurred on a crustal fault within the upper Eurasia plate. At this location, the Philippine Sea plate converges with the Eurasia plate toward the northwest at a rate of 58 mm per year.

Today’s earthquake is located in the same region as a deadly earthquake sequence in April 2016. That sequence included two foreshocks, M 6.2 and M 6.0, followed one day later by a M 7.0 mainshock. The foreshocks to the April 2016 M 7.0 event caused at least nine fatalities and injured more than 800 people, while the M 7.0 mainshock killed at least 40 people immediately from shaking‑related damage, with several hundred additional deaths resulting from injuries and illnesses linked to the earthquake, and injured more than 2,000.Approximately 12,000 houses were damaged or destroyed by the 2016 M7.0 earthquake, and the Aso Ohashi Bridge in Minamiaso collapsed into the Kurokawa River due to a landslide triggered by the quake.

At least 39 people killed, including 9 when a factory chimney collapsed; 166 people injured, including 55 from an explosion at the Aeon Mall Kumamoto; 699 homes destroyed and 8,208 damaged in Kumamoto. Two people injured and 8 houses damaged in Fukuoka. One person injured each in Kagoshima and Oita. Power outages occurred in Kumamoto and a section of a bridge collapsed and fires occurred at Yatsushiro. Widespread water outages occurred in Kumamoto and Nagasaki. Maximum intensity IX. Ground displacement, liquefaction and surface ruptures occurred in Kumamoto. A lava dome partially collapsed and landslides occurred in the Unzen-dake near Shimabara, Nagasaki.
